extracted.intended_audience: scientists and researchers submitting public comments on federal regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientists on drafting effective public comments to federal agencies: what to include, how to present evidence, and how to connect comments to agency mission and statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most valuable comments: unique, fact-based, and succinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The most valuable public comments are unique, fact-based, and succinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must sort through many identical form letters and expressions of personal opinion; distinct, evidence-driven, and concise comments stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage your scientific ability to synthesize data
rubrics_metrics.description: As a scientist, your ability to synthesize data and research is your greatest strength when writing a public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use synthesis of evidence rather than personal opinion; present integrated analysis that helps the agency understand the scientific implications for the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and cite scientific evidence supporting or opposing the regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Your comment can report on scientific evidence that opposes or supports the theory behind the regulation. Providing additional supporting evidence helps strengthen the agency's position by creating a stronger scientific foundation for their action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include empirical data, analyses, and references that directly bear on the regulatory question; providing both supportive and opposing evidence is acceptable if clearly connected to the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include heading with regulation name and docket ID
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a heading that states the regulation name and the docket ID number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this may seem superfluous, it demonstrates that you are taking the time to carefully review the document and be well informed; helps agency staff catalog and locate your comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open by establishing credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an opening sentence to establish your credibility. State who you are and summarize any of your experiences that are relevant to the topic of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise professional identifier (position, expertise, relevant experience) at the start helps agency staff evaluate the weight of your evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a succinct summary of data/research (discussion-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the next few sentences to succinctly summarize the data or research that you have provided. You can (and are encouraged) to go into further detail later in your comment, but starting with the equivalent of a discussion section will help the agency respond more effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a short summary (like a discussion section) so reviewers immediately understand your main evidence and conclusions, then provide supporting detail in subsequent paragraphs or attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly state implications of the research for the regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not have to come to a conclusion or judgement regarding the entirety of the regulation, but you do have to clearly communicate the implications of the research you present. Avoid leaving it up to the agency to infer how research or data relates to the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly connect findings to regulatory questions and possible outcomes; spell out how data should affect the agency's decision or rule language rather than assuming the link is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete citations and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are citing specific papers in your comment, including your sources will help the agency staff find them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full citations and, where possible, links or attachments so staff can quickly access the referenced work; missing citations reduce usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie your comment to the agency's mission and relevant statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Check out the agency's mission statement and any statutes relevant to the regulation. Federal agencies' actions are driven by their mission and held to the standards dictated by statutes, so make your comment stronger by explaining how your information contributes to their mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how your evidence supports or challenges the agency's statutory obligations or mission goals; referencing statutes/mission clarifies legal and policy relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid form letters and unsupported personal opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency will have to sort through many identical form letters and expressions of personal opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit generic form letters or mere personal statements without evidence; such comments are less likely to influence agency decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use templates and exemplary comments for structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Not sure how to structure your comment? We have put together a few broad outlines you can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browse templates and exemplary submitted comments to model structure, tone, and level of detail; emulate strong examples from similar topic areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track agency responses and learn from them
rubrics_metrics.description: You can learn from your own mistakes (and successes) by following up on agency responses to your comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting via Regulations.gov, sign up for email alerts when the agency responds to substantive comments; if the agency responded, analyze how they addressed your points and refine future commenting techniques accordingly.
